searchText: Where I can read about CREATE3 and CREATE4? for create3 you read more [here](https://github.com/0xSequence/create3/) in the initial repo from 0x. [Solmate](https://github.com/transmissions11/solmate/blob/main/src/utils/CREATE3.sol) has an, imho, cleaner implementation though. If you mean new instructions from EOF you can find it here https://notes.ethereum.org/@ipsilon/mega-eof-specification Hey all, I did a bit of a write up on the EOF [here](https://whileydave.com/2023/10/19/digging-into-the-evm-object-format-eof/). Mostly this is just me working through the challenges and trying to understand it all. Anyway, interested in your thoughts. Happy to fix anything that's wrong, etc. > I would guess there are contracts where it is impossible to determine this statically (depending on the byte chosen for the new opcode). There is a lot that could be done to track branch destinations flowing through the stack, memory and storage. Its not clear how far that could be pushed. But, there are situations which are definitely impossible. For example, if a branch destination was returned from a `call` or provided as call data. But, really, I'm looking for clear evidence this approach absolutely could not work. The answer seems to be: *static analysis is probably not good enough to check all jump destinations*. But isn't there anything stronger we can say? Most of the discussion on the jumpdest immediate masking occured 4 years ago. Here's a good ethereum-magicians thread - https://ethereum-magicians.org/t/eip-663-unlimited-swap-and-dup-instructions/3346/10 Ta, I will check that out "Its unclear whether any of these breaking changes caused any significant problems for existing on-chain contracts." - Constantinople was canceled and net gas metering was removed from petersburg because of costing changes EIP-2200 was the fixed variant of net gas metering Ok, I can put something in about that. There were a couple of deployed contracts that broke because of it. Similarly the costing increases of Tangeine whistle broke some contracts, which EIP-2929 fixed via out-of-vm account warming. That was 5 years ago and I lost the reference to the specific contracts. Google may help, but some of it was on that old git based chat channel. Ok, well be great to collect more evidence for the record. I can try and dig out some of that stuff It was driven by older versions of solidity that by default hard coded some gas amounts in some contracts calls based on some huristics that IIRC related to if it was detecing a "pay only" transaciton. also a reserved stiped relating to the amount of gas needed to call SSTORE, used for call failures. So, like `if gas == fixed amount` then do something specific? No, it was limiting the gas it would send to the call. ah yeah, only sending exactly `2300` or something? Recollection is hazy, FEM website may have more details.

excerpts.author: whileydave
excerpts.content:
>  I would guess there are contracts where it is impossible to determine this statically (depending on the byte chosen for the new opcode).
There is a lot that could be done to track branch destinations flowing through the stack, memory and storage.  Its not clear how far that could be pushed.  But, there are situations which are definitely impossible.  For example, if a branch destination was returned from a `call` or provided as call data.

But, really, I'm looking for clear evidence this approach absolutely could not work.  The answer seems to be: *static analysis is probably not good enough to check all jump destinations*.  But isn't there anything stronger we can say?
